extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy / classical ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A normative taxonomy from Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics, Book IV) describing virtues (means) and their corresponding excesses and defects across domains such as wealth, honour, anger, and social intercourse. The page gives character-types, examples, and signs of correct vs faulty dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean regarding wealth: giving and receiving appropriately — not prodigal, not stingy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as giving 'to those to whom he should' and refraining from receiving 'whence he ought not.' Liberality is honourable, purely disinterested, and done in right fashion. The liberal man 'will also spend what he ought, and in right manner.' Anti-patterns: Prodigals give but receive from improper sources and lack self-restraint; Stingy persons fail in giving or accept improper gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prodigality (the Prodigal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive spending/giving: gives openly and lavishly but often receives recklessly from improper sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prodigals are regarded superior to stingy men because they do good to many, but they often combine faults: receiving from improper sources, becoming grasping when means run short, and spending on unrestrained gratification. Their givings may not be honourable or disinterested; they may enrich the wrong people (flatterers) and neglect the respectable. If unguided they 'slide into' faults but can be corrected by care; contrasted with stinginess which is harder to cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stinginess
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect regarding wealth: deficiency of giving or excess of receiving; often incurable and congenial to human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consists of 'defect of giving and excess of receiving' in various modes (sparring, close-fisted, skinflint). Some decline receiving to avoid dishonour; others receive from improper sources (usurers, brothel-keepers) committing base-gaining. Stinginess is called the contrary of liberality and is considered a greater evil than prodigality. Examples/anti-patterns: dicer, robber, usurer as instances of base receiving; skinflint as excess of not-giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue about large-scale, fitting expenditure: spending on great, honourable, public objects in good taste and proportionate to the doer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to expensive, large-scale expenditures (e.g., equipping a trireme, furnishing temples, public spectacles). The Magnificent 'sees what is fitting' and spends with pleasure and without over-accuracy in calculation. Expenditure must be proportionate to the work and to the rank/means of the doer; a poor man attempting it is a fool. The Magnificent prefers beauty/fittingness of the work over mere low cost and spends on durable, honourable public goods. Anti-patterns: Meanness (defect: doing things on too small a scale or with poor taste) and Vulgar Profusion/Want of Taste (excess: spending to display wealth, on improper objects, or in improper manner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanness (relative to Magnificence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect in large-scale expenditure: failing to make fitting, proportionate, or suitably large outlays for honourable public works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Mean man will be deficient, spoiling effects for want of some trifle, procrastinating, contriving to spend the least and lamenting expense. A poor man who overreaches becomes a fool by being out of proportion. Meanness does not necessarily involve disgrace but is faulty in taste and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgar Profusion / Want of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive, improper large-scale spending: lavishing on insignificant objects or for ostentation rather than honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by spending improperly in cases that require small expenditure (e.g., giving a club a feast fit for a wedding, dressing actors in purple for trivial matters). The Vulgar Profuse spends to display wealth and expects admiration; he will spend little where he ought to spend much and much where he should spend little. Faulty because it shows off in improper objects and manner, not merely because of magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great-mindedness (megalopsuchia / the Great-minded man)
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue concerning estimation of one's worth (especially regarding honour): valuing oneself highly and justly — the summit with respect to greatness, combined with thorough goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Great-minded man 'values himself highly and at the same time justly' and is specially concerned with honour (the greatest external good). He bears himself rightly in honour and dishonour, accepts honour moderately from good givers, despises trivial honours, is willing to incur great risks for worthy ends, does kindnesses readily but is ashamed to receive them, overpays to place others under obligation, asks favours reluctantly, behaves loftily toward the great and affably to middling people, prefers reality over appearance, speaks deliberately (slow motion, deep-toned voice), and does not bear malice or boast. Conditions: requires real goodness; imitation without goodness produces insolence/superciliousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect opposite to Great-mindedness: underrating oneself and failing to grasp what one deserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Small-minded are deficient both in estimating themselves and in being esteemed by Great-minded persons; they deprive themselves of deserts through self-ignorance, stand aloof from honourable actions, and are 'laggards.' This defect harms aims, as men's aims are regulated by supposed desert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity / Vain man
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess opposite to Great-mindedness: overestimating oneself without just grounds; foolish self-ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Vain man values himself unduly, attempts honourable things as though worthy and is exposed when detected. He displays circumstances by dress and carriage, seeks visible signs of worth, and talks about his good fortune to receive honour. Vanity is foolish, unlike the praiseworthy Great-mindedness which requires real goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of Honour / Ambition spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispositions regarding pursuit of honour: there is a mean (praised) and extremes (aiming at honour too much from wrong sources or failing to desire honour for what is noble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We blame lovers of honour who aim at it 'more than he ought, and from wrong sources'; we blame those who lack love of honour for not choosing honourable recognition for noble deeds. The mean state has no special name but is praiseworthy. Ambition and lack of love for honour can appear opposed because the mean between them has no dedicated label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meekness (regarding Anger)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean concerning anger: being angry with the right people, about the right things, in the right manner, at the right time, and for the proper length of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meekness is 'being imperturbable' — not led away by passion, but feeling anger as Reason directs. It is often praised and is characterized by moderation: being angry where and when appropriate and not excessively. The mean is difficult to define precisely and depends on particulars and the moral sense. The mean is praiseworthy; slight transgressions towards excess or defect are less blameable than major ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angerlessness / Defect regarding Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect: not being angry when one ought to be; lacking perception and pain, failing to avenge or protect honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who never feel anger at things they should are thought foolish and slavish; bearing scurrility or letting friends suffer without anger is blamed. The defect is sometimes called Angerlessness and leads to failing duties of self-regard or defence of friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess of Anger (over-aptness to anger) and its forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess: being too easily or too often angry, at wrong objects, in excessive degree, too hastily, or for too long a time — manifests in types: Passionate, Choleric, Bitter-tempered, Cross-grained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms: Passionate — soon angry, often excessive but cools quickly; Choleric — excessively vehement, angry at everything; Bitter-tempered — repress anger and keep it long, hard to reconcile; Cross-grained — angry at wrong objects, for too long, and not appeased without vengeance. These excesses are blameable and nuisance to others. The excess is more common than the defect; degree matters for blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-Complaisant (social interchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect in social intercourse: seeks to give pleasure at all costs, agrees to everything, never opposes to avoid causing pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-Complaisant persons agree in everything solely to give pleasure and avoid opposition; they are blameable because they fail to register what ought to be objected. Distinguished from the flatterer who aims to gain profit by pleasing. The mean between Over-Complaisance and Contentiousness is most like Friendship/amiability but is independent of personal affection and guided by propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross / Contentious (social interchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess in social intercourse: opposes everything, indifferent to giving pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross and Contentious people take the contrary line to Over-Complaisant: they oppose in everything and do not care whether they give pain. The mean is praiseworthy: the person 'lets pass what he ought' and 'objects in like manner' according to propriety, avoiding giving pain when it is unseemly or harmful and preferring to give pleasure regulated by nobility and expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean social character (amiable/proper intercourse)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unnamed mean between Over-Complaisant and Contentious: a stable disposition to regulate social intercourse by propriety — give pleasure rather than pain, but guided by what is noble and expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized as 'most like Friendship' — an amiable friend with strong earnest affection yet independent of personal feeling. He regulates intercourse by knowledge of others, giving each his due, inflicting trifling pain if it leads to consequent pleasure, and differing treatment for great/ordinary men. The aim is to avoid giving pain and contribute to pleasure with constant reference to what is noble and expedient.
